As of 155 PM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...An unsettled pattern prevails through midweek. 
Expect near average temperatures, with increasingly humid 
conditions, and daily chances of showers and storms.

Latest surface analysis reveals 1024+ mb high pressure 
remaining well offshore near Bermuda this afternoon. To the 
west, a slow-moving low pressure system continues to drift NE 
across the Ohio River Valley, with an associated cold front 
draped across the eastern OH/TN Valleys into the Deep South. 

Aloft, an amplified upper trough tracks toward the region this 
afternoon, with deep SSW flow drawing tropical moisture north 
into the local area. Regional soundings and early afternoon 
mesoanalysis reveal PW values around 2-2.25", with even higher 
values (to ~ 2.50") just to our south expected to push over the
region later this afternoon and tonight as the dampening upper 
trough swings east.

An earlier round of showers lifted across the US-15 corridor in
the VA Piedmont, dropping up to 1" of rain in spots from Louisa
to Farmville to west of South Hill, with locally higher totals 
just outside our CWA to the N and W. Additional isolated to
widely scattered showers have developed as of this writing 
along a differential heating boundary over central VA, as well 
as farther south along a coastal trough over eastern NC. The 
southern activity will continue lifting NNE across south- 
central/SE VA and eastern NC this afternoon. Locally heavy 
rainfall is expected given the deepening moisture profile, and  
while storm motions should remain progressive enough to 
preclude widespread flooding, localized flash flooding remains 
possible where training occurs. Deep-layer shear remains 
relatively weak, but a low-end severe threat continues—primarily
dependent on isolated wet microbursts developing along the 
previously referenced narrow differential heating boundary near 
the I-95 corridor through early this evening. SPC maintains a 
Marginal Risk along and west of I-95, with isolated damaging 
wind gusts as the primary threat. 

Rain chances ramp down for much of the region overnight, leading
to a warm and muggy night. However, the latest CAM guidance 
highlights two main corridors where convective activity could 
persist into the late night hours as additional MCVs embedded in
the SW flow arrive: the VA Piedmont and along the coast. Have 
lingered higher PoPs in these areas a bit longer. Despite 
increasing moisture /IVT of +3-4 StdDev/ along the coast 
supporting a few heavier downpours, antecedent dry conditions 
over the past few days should preclude flash flood issues. 
Farther inland though, flash flood concerns remain a bit elevated
across the Piedmont, where a couple of rounds of rainfall have 
already occurred. The 12z HREF probabilities continue to support
localized 2-3"+ totals of additional rainfall today and 
tonight. Neighborhood probabilities for rain rates exceeding 
1"/hr are above 70% along the US-15 corridor W/NW of the 
Richmond metro, with a low (~10%) probability for 3"/3hr totals 
in that same area. Still not confident enough for any Flood
Watch areas given the relatively limited area of focus, but any
training cells across the piedmont will need to be closely 
monitored this evening.

For Monday, more widespread showers and storms are likely as 
shortwaves attendant to the dampening upper trough lift across 
the area. While guidance varies on exact areal coverage, the 
continued unsettled pattern supports a persistence-based 
forecast featuring a localized heavy rain threat and an 
isolated, low-end severe risk. The trough weakens further 
Tuesday and Wednesday, but scattered afternoon and evening 
showers and storms capable of heavy rainfall remain expected as 
deep moisture lingers despite weakening SW flow aloft. 

Given the atmospheric profile characterized by weak 
unidirectional flow and tall, skinny CAPE—localized flash 
flooding will remain a threat each day through Wednesday. 
However, the severe threat should stay low due to poor mid-level
lapse rates, a near-saturated vertical column, and weak shear. 
Days 1-3 (Sunday-Tuesday) remain in a WPC Marginal ERO, as the 
overall flash flood risk remains localized due to the lack of a 
strong large-scale surface boundary. High temperatures will 
average slightly below normal early this week owing to 
widespread cloud cover and daily precipitation. NBM numbers do
look a bit high compared to thickness temperatures, especially
given persistent cloud cover, but have been left more or less 
in place for now with limited change to messaging expected.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A more typical summertime pattern returns for 
the latter half of the week. Isolated to scattered afternoon 
showers and thunderstorms remain possible, with near to slightly
above normal temperatures prevailing through next weekend.

While less widespread than early in the week, more typical
summer time diurnally-driven isolated to scattered convective 
chances return Thurs
